stories.headline: Oil prices tumble as Trump cancels attack on Iran to reach nuclear deal
stories.deck: On Sunday, August 2, OPEC+ approved an oil production quota increase of around 188,000 barrels ⁠per day from September, the producer group said, in a move that ⁠completes the unwinding of a layer of voluntary output cuts.
stories.bodyText:
Oil prices tumbled $4 a barrel on Monday (August 3, 2026) after U.S. President Donald Trump held off on a fresh attack on Iran, seeking to reach a quick deal that would halt Tehran’s nuclear ambitions and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent crude futures slid $4.08, or 4.64%, to $83.85 by 2352 GMT while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude was at $80.66 a barrel, down $4.01, or 4.74%.
Both contracts jumped more than 20% last month after fighting between the U.S. and Iran resumed and as attacks on several tankers around Oman heightened security concerns, deterring shippers from entering the Gulf to load oil. In a sign of de-escalation, Mr. Trump said late on Saturday (August 1, 2026) on his Truth Social platform that Iran and other countries in West Asia had asked for time to complete a deal that would lead to “the Immediate, Complete and Total” reopening of the vital strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat”.
“The bigger focus is whether this week turns into a rinse and repeat of last week — with hopes of a deal collapsing as Iran digs in its heels and continues to leverage its control over the Strait, potentially through an attack on a U.S. base or a tanker transiting the waterway,” IG market analyst Tony Sycamore said.
Two tankers laden with Saudi oil crossed the Bab el-Mandeb Straitout of the Red Sea over the weekend while traffic in the Strait of Hormuz slowed following reports of vessel attacks, shipping data showed on Monday (August 3, 2026). The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations has reported three more tanker attacks since Saturday. On Sunday (August 2, 2026), OPEC+ approved an oil production quota increase of around 188,000 barrels per day from September, the producer group said, in a move that completes the unwinding of a layer of voluntary output cuts.
Due to export disruptions from the Gulf, Russia and Kazakhstan caused by the Iran and Ukraine wars, successive monthly OPEC+ hikes over most of this year have remained largely on paper with little impact on the market.
Published - August 03, 2026 06:52 am IST

stories.headline: Japan confirms joint yen intervention with U.S., signals readiness for more action
stories.deck: The joint intervention is the first since 2011’s coordinated action to weaken ‌the yen after the devastating earthquake in eastern Japan
stories.bodyText:
Japan and the United States conducted coordinated yen-buying intervention and will not hesitate to take further action, Japan’s Finance Ministry said on Monday (August 3, 2026), confirming a rare bilateral action to halt the yen’s slide to fresh 40-year lows.
The news underscores both countries’ resolve to prevent a sell-off in the yen and Japanese government bonds (JGB) from causing global spillovers, such as adding upward pressure on already rising U.S. Treasury yields, analysts say.
The joint intervention is the first since 2011’s coordinated action to weaken the yen after the devastating earthquake in eastern Japan.
In its statement, Japan’s Finance Ministry said Friday’s (July 31, 2026) yen-buying intervention with the U.S. Treasury Department “countered excessive volatility and disorderly movements in the Japanese yen in recent months”.
“The Japanese Ministry of Finance remains attentive and in close communication with our counterparts at the U.S. Treasury,” it added. “We will not hesitate to conduct further joint intervention.”
Preceding the announcement, President Donald Trump said on Sunday (August 2, 2026) the United States was helping Japan to prop up the yen as a sign of friendship and to help the world economy.
“They have a weakening yen, and they wanted a little bit of help. And we’re always there for Japan,” Mr. Trump said in response to a reporter’s query why the U.S. is helping to support the yen.
The dollar suddenly dropped against the yen on Monday (August 3, 2026), reversing gains it made earlier in the session after the confirmation from the U.S. and Japan that they intervened in the currency market. The dollar fell 0.6% against the yen to an intraday low of 156.50 in the Asian morning.
“The joint intervention is the culmination of Japan’s alliance with the United States,” Japan’s top currency diplomat Atsushi Mimura told reporters on Monday (August 3, 2026).
“We will continue to align [currency policy] with the Bank of Japan’s monetary policy,” he said, suggesting the government will work hand in hand with the BOJ in arresting yen falls.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also confirmed Friday’s effort, adding Washington “will not hesitate to participate in further joint intervention.”
“We strongly support Japan’s decisive market and monetary steps to correct the substantial undervaluation of the yen,” Bessent said in a separate statement on X, repeating his calls for further interest rate hikes by the Bank of Japan.
The remarks put the spotlight on the BOJ, which last week kept rates on hold but signaled scope for a rate hike as soon as its next policy meeting in September.
Fed facility available
Japan has been struggling to curb a relentless drop in the yen that pushes up import prices and stokes broader inflation, hitting households’ wallets and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s public approval ratings.
Tokyo’s solo intervention conducted between late April and early May caused only a brief yen rebound. The BOJ’s June rate hike to a 31-year high of 1% also gave the struggling currency little lasting boost.
Before Friday’s (July 31, 2026) confirmed joint intervention with the U.S., Japan may have sold as much as $58.97 billion to buy yen when it intervened in New York markets on Thursday, BOJ data suggested.
Analysts doubt whether the latest round of action could counter structural factors driving down the yen, such as the rising cost of fuel from the Middle East conflict and the still wide Japan-U.S. interest rate differentials.
“The announcement effect of joint intervention is much bigger than solo action by Japan,” though the yen fell after the announcement as it was largely within expectations, said Tsuyoshi Ueno, a senior economist at NLI Research Institute.
“The fundamentals driving yen weakness haven’t changed, so we likely won’t see one-sided yen rises from this intervention.”
In a sign of further Japan-U.S. coordination, Bessent said the United States would consider increasing in coming months the size of the Federal Reserve’s repurchase facility providing temporary dollar liquidity, calling the tool an “important backstop”.
The comment came after the MOF’s rare X post on Saturday (August 1, 2026) that it had “a broad range of tools to address market liquidity needs,” including access to the Fed’s repurchase facility providing temporary dollar liquidity.
The Fed facility, introduced in 2020 to steady markets during the COVID-19 pandemic, allows Japan to raise dollar liquidity without outright sales of U.S. Treasuries, potentially easing funding pressures on Tokyo for intervention.
Published - August 03, 2026 06:35 am IST

stories.headline: 'We'll see how it goes': Trump says Iran talks to begin Monday after halting planned strikes
stories.deck: US President Donald Trump announced negotiations with Iran would begin Monday. Diplomatic efforts involving Gulf nations prompted the halt of planned US military strikes. Mediators are working to revive an understanding regarding the Strait of Hormuz. Trump expressed hope for a negotiated settlement on denuclearisation and the waterway. Iranian officials, however, rejected some accounts of formal…
stories.bodyText:
US President Donald Trump said negotiations with Iran will begin on Monday through intermediaries, signalling a renewed diplomatic push after he said he halted planned US military strikes following outreach by key Gulf nations.
Speaking to reporters aboard Air Force One, Trump said talks would begin on Monday afternoon and expressed hope for a negotiated settlement.
"We are talking to them in the form of a negotiation; it begins tomorrow afternoon, and we'll see how it goes. I'd rather make a deal. I'm not looking to kill people because a lot of people die," he said.
Trump said diplomatic efforts involving Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar and Iran prompted him to call off what he described as a planned "massive attack" on Friday.
He also said he expected an agreement on the Strait of Hormuz and expressed confidence that a deal could be reached on Iran's denuclearisation.
The diplomatic push comes as regional mediators work to revive an understanding between Washington and Tehran. Israeli media reported that intermediaries are trying to restore a memorandum of understanding signed last month to keep the Strait of Hormuz open and free of transit fees for 60 days.
Iranian state media also reported that talks between Iran and Oman on a joint mechanism to manage the strategic waterway were in their final stages.
The earlier framework reportedly broke down over differing interpretations. Trump maintained the strait would remain permanently open, while Tehran said the arrangement preserved Iran's sovereign control over the shipping route.
According to reports, Qatari officials held intensive discussions with Iran, the US and Oman over the weekend before informing Trump that Tehran had accepted a proposal related to the strait. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman also spoke to Trump, urging restraint.
Trump later announced on Truth Social that he was pausing the planned strikes, citing progress in talks on the Strait of Hormuz and Iran's nuclear programme.
However, Iranian military officials rejected Trump's account, calling it false. A source linked to Iran's delegation also told the semi-official Fars News Agency that no formal agreement on the Strait of Hormuz had yet been reached.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Gulf allies remain divided on Iran, with Saudi Arabia advocating restraint while the United Arab Emirates has urged Washington to take stronger military action against Tehran.

stories.headline: Not Dhoni! Moeen Ali names former India fast bowler as cricket's sharpest brain
stories.bodyText:
Former England all-rounder 
Moeen Ali
 has named former India fast bowler and Gujarat Titans head coach 
Ashish Nehra
 as the sharpest cricketing mind he has worked with, placing him ahead of several well-known figures, including MS Dhoni.
Moeen, who has played under some of the game's leading captains and coaches, said his time with Nehra at 
Royal Challengers
 Bengaluru (RCB) during the 2018 and 2019 IPL seasons gave him a clear idea of Nehra's ability to understand and manage the game.
Nehra's coaching journey began with RCB as their bowling coach. The team struggled during his stint, and he faced criticism as RCB failed to perform consistently. However, he was handed a bigger role when he became Gujarat Titans' head coach in 2022. In their debut IPL season, GT won the title, making Nehra the first Indian head coach to lift the IPL trophy.
Since then, Gujarat Titans have missed the playoffs only once in five seasons, despite often starting tournaments without being considered among the favourites.
Speaking on the Beard Before Wicket podcast, Moeen explained what, in his view, makes someone a great cricket thinker.
“For me, a cricketing brain is somebody who knows almost every situation of the game. 
Someone who’s got an answer—or a theory—for every situation. Like, they just talk about all aspects. ‘Why he’s not that good, why he is good, what should happen in this situation, what could happen’,” he said, as quoted by News18.
Moeen added that whether those ideas work every time is not the main point.
“But he’s got something," he added. “And behind that something, there’s either data or evidence. Like, ‘It’s happened before, and this happened, and this is why this can happen.’ So the name I am going to give is Ashish Nehra. He is the coach of Gujarat; I had him at RCB for a couple of years. When it comes to cricket brain, this guy knows what he’s talking about. Knows how to get a team environment going, knows how to deal with people, players, and coaches. Amazing, amazing cricket brain."

stories.headline: Walkers form human chain at Lalbagh to oppose tunnel road in Bengaluru
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Walkers, environmental activists and residents formed a human chain near Lalbagh Rock Sunday morning to protest the proposed tunnel road project, saying it would threaten the botanical garden’s ancient geological heritage, biodiversity, and tree cover.
Organised by Lalbagh Walkers’ Association, the demonstration drew around 50 participants across age groups, who joined hands near the iconic rock formation and urged the state govt to scrap the project. Protesters said Bengaluru’s ecological assets should not be sacrificed for infrastructure development.
BV Sridhar Rao, a member of the association who has been walking in the garden for over 30 years, said successive govts had previously responded to citizens’ concerns instead of treating them as matters of prestige. “There was an earlier proposal for a Metro line and station inside Lalbagh, which would have required felling around 400 trees. There was also a proposal for a multi-level parking facility near Siddapura gate. Citizens opposed both projects, and the govts of the day listened to our concerns and modified or shelved them. This govt too should hear the voice of the people instead of making it a prestige issue,” he said.
Rao said the proposed tunnel road also threatened the Peninsular Gneiss rock formation, estimated to be over 3.3 billion years old.
Parvathi Sriram, state general secretary of the environmental organisation Parisarakkagi Naavu, said the tunnel could irreversibly damage the ancient rock formation and disrupt the city’s groundwater system.
“The tunnel road threatens the layers of this crucial rock formation and, in turn, the groundwater system. Lalbagh is one of the few remaining lung spaces in Bengaluru. A report by an expert team from the Geological Survey of India assessing the tunnel’s impact on Lalbagh is still awaited. The project must be dropped,” she said.
Saying the human chain aimed to raise public awareness about Lalbagh’s ecological and heritage significance, the protesters urged govt to pursue infrastructure projects without compromising the city’s natural assets.

stories.headline: Torrential rain lashes DK; Mundaje records 379mm in 24 hours
stories.deck: Nethravati and Kumaradhara flow close to danger mark; search continues for Bantwal man feared swept away in swollen stream
stories.bodyText:
Mangaluru: As torrential rain continued to lash parts of Dakshina Kannada, Mundaje in Belthangady taluk recorded the district’s highest rainfall of 379mm during the 24 hours ending at 8.45am Sunday. Though the intensity of rain subsided across the district Sunday, Nethravati and Kumaradhara rivers continued to flow close to the danger mark. The district received an average of 100.6mm rainfall during the period, while Mangaluru city received comparatively less rain.
Kalmanja in Belthangady taluk recorded 318mm rainfall and Nellikaru 207mm.
A search operation was launched for a 48-year-old man suspected to have fallen into a stream at Panchakodi in Rayi village of Bantwal taluk Saturday night.
Man swept away in stream
Police suspect that Jeevan Pinto, 48, a resident of Panchakodi House in Rayi, slipped while crossing a footbridge and was swept away in the swollen stream while walking to his father-in-law’s house located a short distance from his residence. Fire and rescue department personnel and Bantwal Rural police are continuing efforts to trace him.
Heavy rainfall on Saturday had caused the Nethravati river to swell to critical levels, but water levels subsided by Sunday morning, easing concerns in Panemangaluru and adjoining areas. 
Several residents of Aladka in Panemangaluru and nearby areas on the banks of the Nethravati shifted to safer places.
Floodwaters entered several houses and establishments in Bantwal and Belthangady. According to the District Disaster Management Authority, two houses were damaged in Dakshina Kannada due to heavy rain in the past 24 hours.Mescom reported damage to 36 electric poles.
Nethravati river continued to flow close to the danger mark Sunday
The water level at the bathing ghat of Kukke Sri Subrahmanya Temple reduced slightly, but temple authorities continued restrictions on devotees entering the river for a holy bath.
Yellow alert issued
The IMD has sounded a yellow alert for the district Monday.
A 30-member NDRF team has been deployed in Bantwal, while a 25-member SDRF team is stationed in Mangaluru taluk. Another 10-member SDRF team has been deployed in Subrahmanya. The district administration has arranged 28 boats for rescue operations.

stories.headline: Bengaluru’s civic woes
stories.deck: It remains to be seen whether clearance drives will lead to long-term solutions
stories.bodyText:
Over the last month, residents of Bengaluru have witnessed the Karnataka government waking up to some age-old problems such as encroached footpaths, garbage blackspots, footpath riding and the like.
Spearheaded by the new Greater Bengaluru Development Minister, Krishna Byre Gowda, back-to-back drives since July 1 saw civic authorities attempt to reclaim the city’s notoriously bad pedestrian infrastructure from encroachments by commercial establishments, street vendors, abandoned vehicles, and garbage dumps — problems that most residents had simply resigned to live with.
Though citizens have welcomed the drives, street vendors argue that they were never given vending zones. Moreover, garbage dumping and blackspots exist mostly due to inefficient waste collection as well as civic apathy. In some cases, dumping is carried out by the civic workers themselves due to the lack of waste transfer stations.
The drive to clear footpaths in the city led to altercations between street vendors and civic authorities; in one such clearance drive in Shivajinagar, miscreants even attacked the officials carrying out the drive. Citizens also reported that several of the encroachments that were cleared were back to how they were days after the clearance drive.
The Minister maintained that the aim was not to displace anyone but to create safe pedestrian infrastructure at least on the arterial roads; he said that vendors could move to the inner roads to continue business. However, street vendor unions have questioned this logic, pointing to the lack of will by successive governments to streamline street vending by assigning ID cards and notifying vending zones, so as to prevent harassment from anti-social elements and enforcement agencies. Mr. Gowda later directed corporation officials to conduct a fresh survey of street vendors as the previous survey had enumerated only a little over 30,000 street vendors, while the actual number exceeds 80,000. He also instructed them to identify vending zones.
In the case of abandoned vehicles, the Minister clarified that the campaign is not aimed at vehicles in regular use, admitting that parking regulations requiring houses to have dedicated parking spaces had not been enforced for decades, resulting in residents having to park their vehicles on public roads.
Lack of planning
Urban planning experts and residents have repeatedly pointed to one lacuna when it comes to Bengaluru: the lack of a long-term vision that can keep pace with the level of growth the city experiences. This, they have argued, applies to many areas, from planning the Namma Metro network, that is yet to reach the Kempegowda International Airport, to ensuring connectivity to Bengaluru’s rapidly expanding boundaries.
To address what is easily the city’s best claim to infamy, its traffic, the Congress Government has pushed for new tunnel roads and flyovers. However, urban experts and citizens’ groups have continuously argued against them, reasoning that the city’s public transport should be strengthened instead of introducing short-term solutions for the growing number of private vehicles.
Another case in point is the city’s way of addressing its water needs. As Bengaluru’s once famed network of lakes has been undermined by infrastructure projects, the government is focussed on bringing solutions from afar. Every drought-hit year threatens the Cauvery dependent-city’s water security.
The State government, under the leadership of the new Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar, is pushing aggressively for the positioning of Bengaluru as a prime investment destination. As Bengaluru continues to function without an elected civic council since 2020, with the State government facing pressure from the Supreme Court to conduct elections this year, the emphasis on mega projects such as tunnel roads is being seen as an attempt to tilt the odds towards the Congress.
But since there is no assurance on when these big-ticket projects would be realised, the slew of new drives to fix basic pedestrian problems are the ones that could provide instant relief to citizens. There is a growing call for the government to improve the quality of life of the citizens by first fixing the basics before moving on to big-ticket projects.

stories.headline: Till 3:30 am and beyond: Can Bengaluru become a 24x7 city?
stories.bodyText:
When the FIFA Club World Cup gave Bengaluru a reason to stay awake until 3:30 am, it also gave the city something to think about. For a few nights, people got a fleeting taste of what an extended nightlife could feel like. The move was temporary, but it has rekindled a much larger question: Is Bengaluru ready to become a full-fledged nightlife city?
The answer isn't a simple yes or no. Stakeholders across government, law enforcement and the hospitality industry believe it depends on whether the city's infrastructure, workforce and security systems can evolve alongside its nightlife ambitions.
There is broad agreement that Bengaluru has the demand and the appetite for a stronger night-time economy. But turning it into a city that truly never sleeps will take far more than keeping pubs open for a few extra hours. It will call for real investment in policing, transport, civic services, workforce planning and public safety so that nightlife can grow only as fast as the city's ability to support it.
‘Bengaluru has the demand and the capacity to support extended nightlife’
The city is ready to embrace a stronger night-time economy, believes Shakir Haq, CEO of NKP Empire Ventures and Vice-President of the Bengaluru Chapter of the National Restaurant Association of India (NRAI).
"Bengaluru is more than capable of supporting an extended nightlife. There is a clear demand, and the industry has the capacity to meet it. While not every restaurant or café would operate through the night, fast-food joints, cafés and quick-service restaurants would thrive. We've seen this work successfully in cities across the world, and Bengaluru itself had a vibrant late-night culture in the past," he says.
According to Shakir, the city is now far better equipped to support late-night operations. "With app-based cabs, designated drivers and stronger surveillance systems, nightlife is more feasible than ever. Bengaluru is evolving into a global city and a major GCC hub, and its nightlife should evolve with it. We've always believed that the more active a city is at night, the safer it becomes," he says. He adds that extended nightlife could boost businesses, create jobs and strengthen Bengaluru's global appeal. "We're optimistic the government is listening to the industry's concerns," he says.
‘The real question is whether nightlife can extend till sunrise’
"Bengaluru already has nightlife for almost the entire year. The real question is whether it can extend nightlife until sunrise, and I believe it can," says Avinash Kapoli, mixologist and co-founder of Kompany Hospitality.
Avinash points out that Bengaluru has emerged as one of India's premier cocktail destinations, with two city bars featured among Asia's Best Bars. Most competing Asian cities, he says, allow establishments to operate until 3 am or 4 am. He believes longer operating hours could boost tourism, generate employment and strengthen Bengaluru's hospitality ecosystem, particularly among international travellers accustomed to vibrant night-time economies. However, he also acknowledges the operational challenges.
"Extended hours would require hospitality businesses to rethink staffing and operations. If timings are increased, there should also be flexibility in licensing so businesses can manage their workforce more effectively," he says.
‘Without more manpower, staff will pay the price’
Jagadish HS, who manages a resto-bar in JP Nagar, says the extended timings during the FIFA Club World Cup did not significantly benefit many establishments. "People came and stayed for longer hours but didn't necessarily spend more on food and drinks," he says. While he believes an everyday late-night culture could eventually become commercially viable, he warns that staffing remains a major concern.
"The hospitality industry already struggles with long working hours and poor work-life balance. Extending operating hours without increasing manpower will take a serious toll on employees' mental and physical health," he says.
‘Security has to remain the top priority’
For the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA), the biggest concern isn't operations but planning. M Maheshwar Rao, Chief Commissioner of the GBA, believes Bengaluru can gradually move towards a late-night economy, provided the transition is phased.
"Running a city through the night always requires considerable effort from the civic agencies, especially the police. As Bengaluru evolves, it should gradually consider permitting certain events to continue late into the night based on need and with proper planning," he says, pointing to initiatives such as the midnight marathon in Whitefield as proof that the city is capable of handling late-night events. According to him, expanding nightlife should happen in a graded manner, with security remaining the top priority.
‘A night-time economy would need more police manpower’
Bengaluru City Police Commissioner Seemant Kumar Singh says the police are not opposed to the idea of a city with an extended nightlife but points out that the current security framework is not designed for round-the-clock operations.
"During the FIFA Club World Cup, when establishments were allowed to stay open late, it certainly put a strain on the police. With a proper shift system, we can manage such situations, but without it, the burden falls on the existing force," he says.
According to the commissioner, sustaining a night-time economy would require a significant increase in police manpower and the introduction of dedicated shift systems. "It's not feasible for the existing force to work 24x7, so increasing personnel strength would be essential. Ultimately, however, this is a policy decision that involves multiple stakeholders," he says. He adds that creating a city that functions through the night would require far more than simply extending pub and restaurant hours. Better street lighting, reliable public transport, sufficient cabs, efficient civic services and coordination between multiple government departments would all be crucial.
What Bengaluru needs to become a 24x7 city:
According to stakeholders, a full-fledged night-time economy would require:
- More police manpower and a dedicated night-shift system
- Robust surveillance and security using technology
- Better street lighting across key commercial areas
- Reliable public transport and adequate late-night cabs
- Coordination between agencies, including police, GBA, transport and civic bodies
- Flexible licensing for hospitality businesses
- Additional staffing and revised work shifts in the hospitality sector 
- Support services such as eateries, tea stalls and emergency services operating through the night

stories.headline: Bengaluru records second-driest July in 108 years as monsoon falters
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 After entering the southwest monsoon season with a healthy rainfall surplus, buoyed by robust pre-monsoon showers, Bengaluru witnessed a dramatic decline in rainfall during July, recording its second-driest July in 108 years. India Meteorological Department’s (IMD) city observatory recorded just 23mm of rainfall during the month, the lowest July total since 1918, when only 18.5mm was recorded.
The prolonged dry spell weakened Bengaluru’s southwest monsoon performance. “At the beginning of July, the city had received cumulative southwest monsoon rainfall of around 70mm. However, with only about 23mm of rainfall recorded during the month, the seasonal total rose to just 94mm. Bengaluru typically receives between 80mm and 100mm of rainfall in July,” said CS Patil, scientist at IMD.
The dry conditions persisted through most of July before parts of Bengaluru received light to moderate rainfall on Saturday. According to IMD, the showers were triggered by an offshore trough along the west coast. “An offshore trough at mean sea level, extending from south Gujarat to Kerala along the west coast, has resulted in widespread rainfall over coastal and Malnad 
Karnataka
. Its influence has also extended to parts of south-interior Karnataka, including Bengaluru. 
However, this is likely to be a short-lived spell. Rainfall activity is expected to weaken again before reviving between Aug 6 and Aug 12. Thereafter, monsoon activity is likely to remain weak for much of Aug,” Patil said.
Despite the exceptionally dry July, Bengaluru’s annual rainfall remains within the normal range, largely because of the abundant pre-monsoon rainfall received earlier this year. “Generally the wettest months for Bengaluru is Aug-Sept and a few extended days in Oct. We are hopeful that with a sustained rainfall extending for a few days during these months, Bengaluru will inch closer to record near normal rainfall,” Patil clarified.

stories.headline: RBI expected to hold rates on Aug 5
stories.bodyText:
MUMBAI: RBI is expected to leave interest rates unchanged at its monetary policy committee meeting on August 5 as economists see little case for an immediate policy move despite rising inflation risks, with rupee being stable, resilient domestic growth and uncertainty over crude oil prices shaping expectations.
High frequency indicators, including industrial output and GST collections, point to resilient domestic activity. The main uncertainty lies abroad. Volatility in West Asia and its effect on crude oil prices remain the chief risk, while concerns over El Nino have receded, reducing the urgency for further monetary easing.
According to Soumya Kanti Ghosh, chief economist, SBI group, “With CPI inflation likely to remain above 5% for the next two quarters and likely average of 5% in FY27, we believe RBI will maintain status quo”. He said that while the MPC may keep rates unchanged, the current backdrop has made soft language costlier. Oil volatility, rupee pressure, caution over external flows, and higher inflation projections make an explicitly dovish message less likely.
Ghosh expects Q1 FY27 real GDP growth to outperform RBI’s earlier projection of 6.6% and come in at around 7.0%. He expects CPI inflation for Q1 at 3.9%, followed by 5.2% in Q2, 5.6% in Q3, and 5.0% in Q4, taking the FY27 average to around 5%.
According to Ghosh, “A rate hold can still move markets if the statement shifts the balance between growth comfort and inflation / FX vigilance”.
He said investors should watch RBI’s intervention in the short end of the forward book, where the short end forward position has reduced by $13 billion, alongside cumulative foreign inflows of around $35 billion through FCNR(B) deposits and other channels. He also pointed to the positive Indian Ocean Dipole, which stood at +0.44 degrees Celsius on July 26. The difference in sea surface temperatures between the western and eastern parts of the Indian Ocean could support rainfall and offset initial monsoon shortfalls.
According to Santanu Sengupta and Arjun Varma of Goldman Sachs, the rupee is expected to stabilise following RBI measures to attract foreign capital. “With the INR having broadly stabilised following the RBI’s recent FX measures, we see limited need for the MPC to turn more hawkish near term”. They expect RBI to lower its inflation forecast modestly as crude oil prices remain below the $95 a barrel benchmark used at the June policy meeting.

stories.headline: Investments in PE-VC fall 6% to $20.3bn in Jan-July
stories.deck: India's private equity and venture capital investments surpassed twenty billion dollars this year. This figure shows a slight decrease compared to the previous year's performance. July saw investments of three billion dollars, remaining stable from last year's figures. Investors maintain long-term confidence in India's private markets despite global challenges. Sectors like renewable energy and…
stories.bodyText:
CHENNAI: Private Equity-Venture Capital (PE-VC) in India crossed $20 billion mark in Jan-July this year (CY2026). However, it is nearly 6% lower than $21.5 billion recorded in the corresponding seven month period (Jan-July) last year (CY2025) .
July 2026 recorded an investment of $3 billion, which is flat against $3.2 billion in the same month in 2025, data released by research firm Venture Intelligence showed. Global investment firm Brookfield’s Lumara, a renewable energy platform, led the PE-VC investments deals in July, with an investment of about $600 million. It took the cumulative investments to $20.3 billion this year comprising 756 deals. The PE-VC investments do not include those relating to the real estate sector.
Arun Natarajan, founder, Venture Intelligence said, the investments highlighted the continued long-term faith global and domestic investors have in India’s private markets, amid geopolitical challenges and volatile public markets depressing IPO activity. 
“Healthy exits notched up by investors in recent months — including via the Meta-CRED deal and public market sales — offer a strong reason for optimism,” he told TOI.
In recent months, PE investors are laying emphasis on sectors, such as infrastructure (especially renewable power companies), manufacturing (automobile and auto components in particular) and data centres, apart from the traditional sectors like NBFCs and healthcare. 
“VC investors are doubling down on B2B software startups, including special emphasis on AI-enabled companies like Sarvam AI and Emergent Labs,” he added.
Natarajan said, private markets in India showed an impressive resilience across H1 2026. “So long as global macro conditions stay relatively stable, the total PE-VC deployment this year can be expected to land roughly on par with 2025,” he said.

stories.headline: Education needs more capital, fewer curbs: Noel Tata
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata on Sunday questioned restrictions on for-profit education, saying they discouraged investment in a sector where India needs far more quality colleges and universities.
Speaking at IIMBue, an IIM Bangalore alumni meet in Bengaluru, Tata said only a small fraction of students secure admission to the country’s top institutions, forcing many high-performing students to pursue higher education overseas.
“We spend an atrocious amount of money every year sending kids to the US and Europe,” he said.
Tata said India should create enough world-class institutions so students do not have to leave the country for quality education and career opportunities.
“I believe the courts have said that you can’t. An educational institution cannot be for profit, which is sad,” he said. “I think it’s preventing a lot of money from coming into education, into building the education system.”
His remarks come as Tata Trusts partners with IIM Bangalore to establish its School of Undergraduate Studies. Tata said education would be a key focus area for the Trusts, which wants to return to building institutions as it did with the Indian Institute of Science, Tata Institute of Fundamental Research and Tata Memorial Hospital.
“I’d like to start spending some more of our money on building new institutions,” he said.
Healthcare is another priority. Tata said the Trusts plans to build 40-50 general hospitals across India.
“We’re now looking to see if we can build 40 or 50 general-purpose hospitals across India,” he said. “We’ve identified three locations. We’re going to start that.”
The hospitals will operate on a not -profit basis and aim to work within the funding available under govt health insurance schemes.
The Trusts is also considering a cross-subsidy model under which 20-30% of rooms would be charged at commercial rates, helping subsidise treatment for the remaining patients.
Tata said all patients would receive the same doctors, medicines and operating theatres. Those paying more would primarily get private rooms and additional facilities for their families.
He also called for more rigorous ways to measure the impact of philanthropy, questioning broad claims that projects had “touched” thousands of lives without demonstrating what had actually changed. “We need to be clear about what we mean when we say ‘touch the lives of somebody’,” he said.

stories.headline: West Asia war uncertainty keeps businesses on edge
stories.deck: Businesses face significant cost management challenges due to ongoing West Asia conflict. Commodity inflation and freight charges create persistent planning uncertainties for companies. This instability may lead to postponed capital deployment and fewer new job additions. Consumers can expect widespread price increases across various products and services. Companies are considering further…
stories.bodyText:
MUMBAI: A prolonged war in West Asia is making it difficult for companies to manage their costs—the persistent volatility be it in terms of commodity inflation, freight charges or exchange rates means nothing can be planned with certainty. While rising costs will squeeze margins, some of the businesses are also wary that discretionary demand may take a hit amid multiple rounds of price increases. 
“For companies like ours, the biggest uncertainties stem from volatility in commodity prices/raw material costs, freight costs and shipping timelines, all of which can impact supply chain planning. It forces us to double down on execution, enforce cost-discipline and diversify sourcing,” said Shrikant Kanhere, MD & CEO at AWL Agri Business.
Pricing products is becoming a challenge because there is no stability in rates, said Mayank Shah, chief marketing officer at Parle Products. 
Continued uncertainty will push companies to postpone capital deployment weighing on fresh job additions and broader demand, said B. Thiagarajan, MD at Blue Star. “This whole FY will be strained. When costs go up, both margins and consumer demand get impacted,” Thiagarajan said. 
In their recent quarterly earnings, companies have said that commodity inflation continues to be a major headwind, projecting more price hikes going ahead. 
“A protracted conflict in West Asia, alongside emerging El Nino conditions that may weaken monsoons and intensify heatwaves, could weigh on growth, inflation and current account,” ITC said, highlighting trade and supply chain disruptions in Q1.
Prolonged geopolitical conflicts may increase uncertainty for businesses in the short-term, said Ashok Nair, MD, RPG Life Sciences, adding that the firm’s continued expansion into new and emerging markets offers it some operational buffers. For consumers, supply chain volatility will translate into more price hikes across the board, potentially making festive shopping pricier. “.....if need be we will also make further pricing interventions because we’re also coming to terms with the exact inflationary impact on the margins,” said Ashish Goenka, group CFO at Tata Consumer Products in recent earnings call.
Mohit Malhotra, global CEO at Dabur India said inflationary pressures are expected going forward.

stories.headline: China gets just 1 FDI approval in India in FY26, Hong Kong secures 13 proposals
stories.deck: India approved only one Chinese FDI proposal worth one crore rupees in 2025-26. Hong Kong received approvals for thirteen proposals totaling six hundred ten crore rupees. Singapore led approved investment values with three thousand two hundred fifty-nine crore rupees. The UK and Thailand also saw significant investment approvals during this period. China's overall FDI contribution to India…
stories.bodyText:
China's share in India's foreign direct investment (FDI) approvals remained largely negligible in 2025-26, with the government approving just one proposal worth Rs 1 crore during the year. In comparison, 13 proposals from Hong Kong, together worth Rs 610.42 crore, received approval, according to official data. 
These approvals fall under India's investment screening rules for countries sharing a land border with the country. Introduced through Press Note 3 of the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) in April 2020, the policy requires prior government approval for such investments. The regulations were brought in during the Covid-19 pandemic to curb opportunistic takeovers and acquisitions of Indian companies.
During April 2025 to March 2026, the government approved 63 FDI proposals with a total investment value of Rs 10,292.67 crore ($1.18 billion), according to DPIIT data.
Among all countries whose proposals were cleared, Singapore accounted for the highest approved investment value. 
Five proposals from the country worth Rs 3,259.88 crore ($382.52 million) received approval.
The UK followed with five proposals worth Rs 2,477.67 crore ($283 million), while two proposals from Thailand valued at Rs 1,600 crore (about $180 million) were also cleared.
Press Note 3 eased
Back in March, the government revised certain provisions of Press Note 3, allowing investors with non-controlling beneficial ownership of up to 10% from land border countries (LBCs) to invest through the automatic route, subject to applicable sectoral caps, entry routes and other conditions.
However, the relaxation does not extend to entities registered in China, Hong Kong or any other country sharing a land border with India. The countries sharing land borders with India are China, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Bhutan, Nepal, Myanmar and Afghanistan.
China remains a small source of FDI
Official data also shows that China has remained a relatively small contributor to India's overall FDI inflows. Between April 2000 and March 2026, the country ranked 23rd among FDI sources, accounting for only 0.32% of India's total FDI equity inflows. During the period, Chinese investments totalled $2.51 billion, or Rs 16,162.25 crore.
Hong Kong ranked 15th over the same period, with a 0.62% share in total FDI equity inflows into India. Cumulative investments from the territory stood at $4.91 billion, equivalent to Rs 31,220.30 crore.
The latest approvals are broadly in line with the previous financial year.
In 2024-25, India had also approved only one FDI proposal from China. That proposal was valued at Rs 28.71 crore ($3.44 million). 
Overall, the government had cleared 82 proposals under the government route during the year, involving investments worth Rs 39,758 crore ($4.72 billion).
Hong Kong, meanwhile, received approvals for 11 proposals worth Rs 1,225.28 crore ($146.51 million) during 2024-25.

stories.headline: Glasgow bids farewell to Commonwealth Games with handover to Ahmedabad
stories.deck: Overall, it was a fitting finale to a glitzy show that seamlessly blended the finest of Scotland’s music, culture and heritage with India’s rich traditions that showcased the shared values of unity, friendship and hospitality that perhaps best define the Commonwealth spirit
stories.bodyText:
As Glasgow bid farewell to the Commonwealth Games with a grand and colourful closing ceremony at the OVO Hydro here on Sunday (August 2, 2026), perhaps no words captured the spirit of the host city better than those of celebrated Scottish poet Jackie Kay.
In a moving love letter to Glasgow, with a backdrop of videos showing residents at the city’s iconic landmarks, Kay posed a simple yet profound question: “....What is Glasgow if not a place of welcome to the citizens of the world?”
It was a sentiment that resonated throughout the 11-day Games, during which the Scottish city earned widespread praise for its warmth, kindness, hospitality and impeccable organisation.
The ceremonial handover of the Commonwealth Games flag to Olympic and World champion Neeraj Chopra and Indian Olympic Association president P. T. Usha and the Deputy Chief Minister of Gujarat, Harsh Sanghavi, accompanied by the voice of Scottish singer Shereen Cutkelvin, symbolically transferred the Games from Glasgow to Ahmedabad, host of the 2030 (centenary) Games.
When India took over the cultural show from Glasgow, the Indian audience erupted in joy.
Titled ‘The World is One Family: Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam’, the opening ensemble celebrated the enduring Indian philosophy of universal brotherhood while commemorating the 150th anniversary of the national song Vande Mataram. Led by actress and former Miss World Manushi Chhillar, with a musical score by Shankar Mahadevan and choreography by Shiamak Davar and his troupe, the performance presented India’s rich cultural heritage and its message of unity and hospitality to the world.
Shankar Mahadevan’s sons Shivam and Siddharth, along with the energetic performance of renowned Gujarati and Bollywood playback singer Bhoomi Trivedi, added more vibrancy and heft to the spectacle and brought the Indian segment alive on the Glasgow stage.
Earlier, singer-songwriter Sandi Thom set the tone for the night with the song ‘Proud to Be From Scotland’, accompanied by the tribal drum band Clann An Drumma.
Australian singer Delta Goodrem then welcomed the athletes with a medley of her greatest hits as volunteers carrying the flags of the 74 participating nations and territories entered the arena. She followed it with a stirring rendition of Warrior, accompanied by archive footage celebrating memorable moments from the Games.
Goodrem later invited Scottish singer Cammy Barnes onto the stage, and the duo performed John Farnham’s popular anthem ‘You’re the Voice, backed by a choir and traditional Scottish pipers, drawing one of the loudest ovations of the evening.
The celebrations gathered further momentum as Primal Scream’s hit ‘Loaded’ came alive through a fine collaboration featuring bagpipers, community performers and Glaswegian-Nigerian rapper Bemz.
The mood then turned reflective with Jackie Kay’s poignant poem before the spotlight shifted to electro-trad band ‘Elephant Sessions’. Their pulsating performance, accompanied by poet and musician Hamish Kiernan-Hutcheson, showcased Glasgow’s vibrant contemporary spirit.
Later, Scotland’s para-athlete Melanie Woods received the David Dixon Award, presented to the outstanding athlete of the Commonwealth Games in recognition of excellence in performance, fair play and overall contribution to her team’s campaign.
Overall, it was a fitting finale to a glitzy show that seamlessly blended the finest of Scotland’s music, culture and heritage with India’s rich traditions that showcased the shared values of unity, friendship and hospitality that perhaps best define the Commonwealth spirit.
Published - August 03, 2026 04:01 am IST

stories.headline: Had to prove that I deserved to be part of Asian Games team: Ankur Bhattacharjee
stories.deck: While India, as hosts, fielded 16 players in the singles events — prompting many to jokingly refer to the tournament as the “India Open” — Ankur arrived only because of the expanded quota. Yet his path to the title was anything but straightforward
stories.bodyText:
The moment he blocked one of Payas Jain’s signature forehand topspins from the backhand corner deep into the forehand corner and watched his doubles partner fail to reach it, Ankur Bhattacharjee knew the wait was over.
The 19-year-old dropped his racquet, turned to the near-capacity crowd of over 2,000 — largely made up of schoolchildren — and gestured at them to raise the volume. He then blew a flying kiss towards the stands before embracing Payas and sharing a long hug with his father-cum-coach Angshuman Bhattacharjee.
It was more than the celebration of a title.
By prevailing in a topsy-turvy 70-minute final to win the men’s singles crown at the 22nd Commonwealth Table Tennis Championships, Ankur had delivered his answer to the Indian table tennis fraternity.
Less than a fortnight after narrowly missing out on India’s squads for both the Commonwealth Championships and, more significantly, the Asian Games, the Kolkata paddler had produced perhaps the finest week of his seniors career.
“For me, this was the most important event of my life,” Ankur told The Hindu after posing for dozens of selfies and signing more than a few autographs at the Thyagaraj Sports Complex on Sunday (August 2, 2026) night.
“I had to prove to myself and to everyone else that I deserved to be part of the Indian team. I deserved to be part of the Asian Games team.”
The irony was impossible to ignore.
While India, as hosts, fielded 16 players in the singles events — prompting many to jokingly refer to the tournament as the “India Open” — Ankur arrived only because of the expanded quota. Yet his path to the title was anything but straightforward.
His round of 16 itself was against Malaysia’s Wong Qi Shen, the man who had stunned both Manav Thakkar and Manush Shah during the team championships and almost single-handedly threatened India’s supremacy.
Ankur dismantled him 4-0.
Next came Australia’s Nicholas Lum, the World No. 44 and third seed, a left-hander who had beaten Ankur the last time they met. This time, the Indian matched Lum for pace, repeatedly using his trademark backhand winners and flat punches to deny the Australian any rhythm.
“I had lost to Lum in our last meeting. So for me, if I wanted to win this tournament, I had to be at my best,” Ankur said.
Then came Manav Thakkar in the semifinals, arguably India’s biggest title contender. Having faced him during Ultimate Table Tennis last month, Ankur carried a clear tactical blueprint into the contest.
“Recently I played against Manav in UTT, so I knew how to play against him.”
More importantly, he showcased the aspect of his game that has improved the most over the last six months. Long regarded as one of India’s finest backhand players, Ankur repeatedly breached Manav’s defensive wall with his forehand as well, underlining the strides he has made under father-cum-coach Angshuman’s guidance.
The final, however, demanded something entirely different. Across the table stood Payas, not merely another Indian youngster but his regular doubles partner, practice companion and a friend. The familiarity only made the contest harder.
“He is my doubles partner. We are very good friends,” Ankur said. “We always practise together. He knows my weak points and I know his. Even our mental trainer (Vir Saran) is the same.”
The chess match lasted 70 engrossing minutes before Ankur recovered from 2-3 down to prevail in seven games. “I was very happy that I played against him in the final. And I am very happy that I won the title.”
Beyond the trophy, though, the week represented validation. “I had never been part of the Commonwealth Championships team. I came here only for the individual events,” he said. “So the first thing was to prove that I can be part of the Indian team.”
The omission from the Asian Games squad inevitably added motivation, though Ankur insisted it wasn’t the only driving force.
“I don’t really care whether I’m in the Asian Games or not. I always want to win every tournament I play. Whatever tournament it is, I take it seriously.”
Then, after a brief pause, he admitted the criticism had fuelled him.
“I like such challenges when people doubt me. Maybe a lot of people think I have only come because I am the host country’s player. But I feel that if I play well consistently, I can beat anyone.”
Asked about the flying kiss immediately after championship point, the otherwise animated teenager suddenly turned shy. “My mother,” he said with a sheepish smile. No doubt his mother Kuntali — also a former paddler just like his father — was praying while sitting in the stands, sitting next to her was a friend.
There is little time to savour the biggest title of his young career. His next stop is Europe Smash in Sweden starting over the weekend, where another opportunity awaits against the world’s elite. “Now I’ll head to Europe Smash,” Ankur said. “I hope I can return with a medal.”
Published - August 03, 2026 03:17 am IST

stories.headline: India secure top-four finish at 2026 Commonwealth Games after historic 39-medal campaign
stories.deck: India finished fourth at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow with 39 medals (13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze), despite failing to add to their tally on the final day. A record 16-medal haul on Saturday sealed their position, with boxing leading the charge. The campaign also featured several historic milestones ahead of the 2030 Games in Ahmedabad.
stories.bodyText:
India signed off from the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow without adding to their medal tally on the final day, ending the campaign with 39 medals (13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze) to finish fourth overall. The Indian contingent had effectively secured its place in the standings after a record-breaking 16-medal haul on Saturday, the country's biggest single-day return of the Games.
 Australia once again topped the medals table with a dominant 171 medals (70 gold, 50 silver and 51 bronze), while England finished second with 110 medals (28 gold, 45 silver and 37 bronze). Canada claimed third with 62 medals (18 gold, 21 silver and 23 bronze). India finished fourth on 39 medals, ahead of hosts Scotland, who also collected 39 medals but finished below India because of a lower silver-medal count.
 Despite failing to add another podium finish on the final day, India completed one of its strongest Commonwealth Games campaigns in recent years. A total of 122 athletes represented the country in Glasgow, with 38 athletes returning home with medals, including Gulveer Singh, who became India's only double medallist after winning bronze in both the men's 10,000m and 5,000m.
Final day brings near misses across multiple sports 
India came closest to adding another medal through Ishroop Narang in women's -78kg judo. Narang kept her medal hopes alive by defeating Georgika Wesley Djengue Moune of Cameroon in the repechage to reach the bronze-medal contest. However, she narrowly missed the podium after losing the bronze bout to Canada's Coralie Godbout, ending India's judo campaign just short of another medal.
India end the 2026 Commonwealth Games on a high, finishing fourth with 39 medals after a historic campaign led by boxing and several landmark performances.
In the men's -81kg category, Harsh Tokas remained in contention after defeating Peniamina Percival of Samoa in the repechage. He progressed into the bronze-medal match but was beaten by Australia's Keishin Ochi, finishing just outside the medals.
India's other judokas exited earlier in their campaigns. Avtar Singh lost to Aristos Michael of Cyprus in the men's -100kg Round of 16, while Yash Ghanghas was eliminated by Joshua Whitehouse in the men's +100kg Round of 16.
Cyclists unable to break into medal positions
 India's cyclists endured a difficult final day without reaching the podium.
Ronaldo Singh Laitonjam fell out of medal contention in the men's 1000m Time Trial final after failing to challenge the leading riders.
In the men's 40km Points Race first round, Dinesh Kumar and Harshveer Singh Sekhon were both eliminated before the medal races, bringing India's track cycling campaign to a close.
Lisha Das finishes sixth in para cycling
 India's lone para cycling representative on the final day, Lisha Das, finished sixth in the women's C4-C5 1000m Time Trial final.
 Das had also narrowly missed qualification for the 4000m Individual Pursuit finals earlier in the Games and concluded her Glasgow campaign with two respectable performances against a strong international field.
Historic 16-medal haul had already secured fourth place
 India's position in the standings had effectively been sealed by Saturday's spectacular 16-medal surge — the country's best single-day performance of the Games.
The highlight came inside the boxing ring, where India produced an extraordinary 10-medal return, winning seven golds and three silvers.
The gold medals came through:
- Sakshi Chaudhary (women's 51kg), who defeated England's Ruby White.
- Preeti Pawar (women's 54kg), who beat Canada's Scarlett Savannah Delgado.
- Jaismine Lamboria (women's 57kg), who overcame Northern Ireland's Michaela Walsh.
- Priya Ghanghas (women's 60kg), who defeated Canada's Marie-Bathoul Al-Ahmadieh.
- Arundhati Choudhary (women's 70kg), who beat England's Chantelle Reid.
- Sachin Siwach (men's 60kg), who defeated Namibia's Tryagain Morning Ndevelo.
- Ankush Panghal (men's 80kg), who claimed gold after beating England's Dimeji Shittu.
India's boxing silver medallists were:
- Lovlina Borgohain (women's 75kg), who lost to Australia's Emma Sue Greentree in the final.
- Jadumani Singh (men's 55kg), who finished runner-up to Australia's Jye Dixon.
- Narender Berwal (men's 90+kg), who settled for silver after losing to England's Damar Thomas in the final.
**EDS: THIRD PARTY IMAGE** In this image received on Aug. 2, 2026, members of the Indian boxing contingent including Jaismine Lamboria, Lovlina Borgohain, Sakshi Chaudhary, Arundhati Choudhary, Sachin Siwach and Ankush Panghal pose for photographs after the boxing events at the 23rd Commonwealth Games (CWG), in Glasgow, Scotland. (Handout via PTI Photo) (PTI08_02_2026_000056B) *** Local Caption ***
Para athletics also delivered a memorable double podium in the men's F57 shot put. Soman Rana won gold with a season-best 13.40m, finishing ahead of teammate Shubham Juyal, whose 13.28m secured silver for India.
Athletics added another double podium through the men's triple jump, where Praveen Chithravel claimed silver with 16.58m, finishing behind Jamaica's Jordan Scott (16.72m), while teammate Selva Prabhu Thirumaran earned bronze with 16.52m.
Gulveer Singh completed India's medal tally for the day by winning bronze in the men's 5,000m in 13:24.95, narrowly edging Cornelius Kemboi of Kenya by just 0.04 seconds after finishing behind Australia's Ky Robinson and Kenya's Michael Kiplangat Kipsang.
Glasgow campaign delivers historic firsts and fresh milestones
 India's 39-medal campaign featured several landmark achievements despite the absence of traditional medal-rich sports such as shooting, wrestling, badminton, hockey and table tennis from the programme.
Boxing emerged as India's biggest contributor with 10 medals, reinforcing the country's growing dominance in the sport at the Commonwealth Games.
Judo produced breakthrough moments as Asmita Dey and Harsh Singh became India's first Commonwealth Games judo gold medallists, while Tejaswin Shankar became the first Indian ever to win a Commonwealth Games decathlon medal with bronze.
The athletics team also produced memorable performances through 
Neeraj Chopra
, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu Thirumaran, Yash Vir Singh and Gulveer Singh, while India's para athletes delivered multiple podium sweeps across the competition.
With the Glasgow Games now concluded, attention turns to the 2030 Commonwealth Games in Ahmedabad, where India will host the event for the second time after New Delhi 2010. During the closing ceremony, the Commonwealth baton will officially be handed over to India, with boxing gold medallist Jaismine Lamboria serving as the country's flag bearer after one of the most successful campaigns in India's Commonwealth Games history.

stories.headline: Jamshedpur FC pulling out of ISL a punch in the gut: Sunil Chhetri
stories.deck: Jamshedpur FC, winners of the ISL Winners' Shield in the 2021-22 season, had announced their withdrawal from the ISL on July 31 just hours after missing the deadline for payment of participation fee for the upcoming season, beginning September 4
stories.bodyText:
Indian football legend Sunil Chhetri has expressed his anguish over Indian Super League side Jamshedpur FC's decision to pull out of the upcoming season, describing the development as "a punch in the gut" and urging the club's management to reconsider.
Jamshedpur FC, winners of the ISL Winners' Shield in the 2021-22 season, had announced their withdrawal from the ISL on July 31 just hours after missing the deadline for payment of participation fee for the upcoming season, beginning September 4.
In a post on Instagram, the club had confirmed that it would not participate in the ISL from the 2026-27 season onwards. The upcoming season will now feature 13 teams.
"To know that Jamshedpur has folded first team operations is a punch to the gut. The players and staff will be without clubs, and they might find one by the end of it all. The League will have a team less, but the season will go on," wrote Chhetri, India's all-time top goalscorer, most-capped player, and the fourth-highest international goalscorer in men's football history.
"However, not having the TATA group involved in the top tier of Indian football — that would be a disaster with no alternative," he added.
Jamshedpur FC, which made its ISL debut in 2017, however said in its statement that Jamshedpur Football and Sporting Private Limited (JFSPL) would continue to promote and develop the sport at the grassroots level despite the club's withdrawal from the league.
Chhetri lauded the Tata Group for its contribution to Indian football, first through the Tata Football Academy (TFA) and later by establishing and nurturing Jamshedpur FC.
"It takes a lot to be a stakeholder in Indian football. It has been like that for some time now. But when everything around looks like it will crumble, you bank on family to hold on to each other. And more often than not, it is the elders in the house that you turn to, for assurance. All of you at the TATA Group, through TFA first, and then @JamshedpurFC , have been one of our pillars."
The decision to withdraw is understood to have been influenced by the All India Football Federation's (AIFF) directive requiring clubs to pay an administrative fee of Rs 1.1 crore in two instalments. According to sources, the club's board of directors has also decided to wind up the senior team for the time being.
"I understand that some tough decisions in sport are down to what makes sense in the board room. But I can only request and hope that the think tank at TATA picks their heart over head and reconsiders this call. It might be a poor business decision, but it will be the one Indian football needs the most at this hour," added the Bengaluru FC stalwart.
Published - August 03, 2026 01:28 am IST

stories.headline: Gulveer Singh’s 'double' speaks of patience and precision
stories.deck: Runner Turned Untapped Potential Into 10,000m & 5,000m Medals For CWG History
stories.bodyText:
Few combinations in athletics are as revered — or as punishing — as the 5000m and 10,000m. Yet India’s Gulveer Singh rode both challenges in Glasgow, adding a bronze in the 5000m to the silver he had claimed in the 10,000m days earlier to script one of Indian athletics’ finest Commonwealth Games campaigns.
In doing so, Gulveer became the first Indian to win two athletics medals at a single Commonwealth Games, leaving long-time coach Scott Simmons beaming with pride.
“Honestly, all I knew after meeting the Indian distance runners at SAI Bengaluru was that they had a lot of untapped potential,” Simmons told TOI from Glasgow on Sunday.
That potential was on full display in Glasgow. If the 10,000m tested Gulveer’s endurance, the 5000m demanded patience and precision — qualities he displayed throughout the race.
Staying on the inside rail to cover the shortest possible distance, Gulveer remained between third and eighth spots for much of the race, resisting the temptation to make unnecessary moves.
It was all part of the plan.
“It was important not to get boxed in or behind with so many runners, and so many very good runners, in one heat,” Simmons explained.
Then when eventual winner Mathew Kipchumba Kipsang of Kenya surged into the lead at the start of the final lap, Gulveer bided his time, waiting for the right moment to launch his challenge. 
Simmons knew his ward possessed the finishing speed to make patience pay.
“What has impressed me the most is his last 400m, 200m and 100m finishing speed. I didn’t see that coming until his 5K at LA Track Fest this spring, where he ran 13:03.93. He was able to outkick true 1500m/5000m runners off a relatively fast pace,” Simmons said.
With about 200 metres remaining, the battle for the remaining two podium places came down to Gulveer, Australia’s Ky Robinson and Kenya’s Cornelius Kemboi. For a brief moment, it appeared Gulveer would claim silver, with Kemboi settling for bronze.
However, Robinson, the 10,000m champion, produced a brilliant late kick to snatch silver, while Gulveer did just enough to hold off Kemboi and secure bronze in 13:24.95, completing a historic Commonwealth Games campaign.
Despite the short turnaround between the two races, Simmons revealed there was little deviation from the routine that had helped Gulveer arrive in Glasgow in peak condition. “After the 10,000m silver, we approached recovery like we always do with a focus on sleep, massage, diet and, very importantly, easy aerobic running,” he said.
Simmons, however, believes there is still plenty of room for the 28-year-old Indian to improve.
“While Commonwealth Games is one of the competitive arenas for long-distance running, the World Championships and Olympic Games are even tougher. Gulveer needs to continue to improve, especially his finishing kick,” he added.
At the same time, the American coach believes his success can inspire a new generation of Indian distance runners, provided they receive the right support.
“I think Gulveer’s success will change the belief system of Indian distance runners,” said Simmons, who also coached Avinash Sable to the men’s 3000m steeplechase silver at Birmingham Commonwealth Games.
“Do I think other Indians can get to this level? Of course, as long as they have the support for training and competitions abroad and are willing to commit and sacrifice and not look for shortcuts.”
